Maladaptive Strategies.value: I spend long hours on my phone, games, or internet to avoid thinking
Places of worship or religious gatherings
Crowded places such as shopping centres or public events

Memory.value: My memories of the event come in disconnected pieces that do not fit together
My memories of the frightening event are like a film that plays over and over.
I know what happened but I am unable to find words to describe it

Negative Appraisals.value: I am not sure my life is worth living anymore
The world is a dangerous place

issues.item: Memory: Verbal Access: I can talk about what happened very easily.
issues.explanation: Within the Memory node, 'Verbal Access' directly conflicts with the combination of 'Fragmented Pieces' and repetitive intrusive replay. A patient who says the trauma memory is fragmented and involuntarily replayed would not usually also report being able to talk about it very easily; this is a hard within-node contradiction rather than normal heterogeneity.

issues.item: Memory: Fragmented Pieces: My memories of the event come in disconnected pieces that do not fit together.
issues.explanation: The maladaptive avoidance items are not clinically well anchored to the rest of the profile or to the military trauma context presented here. Avoiding enclosed spaces and religious spaces suggests specific situational trigger-linked avoidance, but the profile contains no Triggers items and the formulation explicitly leaves Triggers disconnected from the other active components. These avoidance choices therefore do not fit the stated formulation and are hard to connect to the memory/appraisal pattern that is otherwise driving symptoms.

issues.item: Memory: Memory Replay: My memories of the frightening event are like a film that plays over and over.
issues.explanation: Negative appraisals are generally severe and coherent with high PTSD burden, but because the active formulation centers Negative Appraisals driving Maladaptive Strategies and Memory, the selected maladaptive strategies should plausibly arise from those appraisals. 'Screen Escape' fits this, whereas avoidance of enclosed and religious spaces does not clearly follow from the selected appraisals ('Constant Vigilance,' 'Life Not Worth Living,' 'No Accountability').

issues.item: Avoid Enclosed Spaces: Enclosed or confined spaces
issues.explanation: The maladaptive avoidance items are not clinically well matched to the rest of the profile or to a military trauma formulation here. Avoiding enclosed spaces and religious spaces suggests highly specific trigger-linked avoidance, but the profile contains no Trigger items and no Threat content tied to confinement, ambush, captivity, worship settings, or comparable trauma cues. This makes these two avoidance items feel disconnected from the reported memory and appraisal pattern.

issues.item: Avoid Religious Spaces: Places of worship or religious gatherings
issues.explanation: 'Constant Vigilance' implies an active current-sense-of-threat/hypervigilance presentation. In this formulation, Threat is not active and Negative Appraisals has no link to Threat; the rest of the selected items center more on fragmented/repetitive memory, injustice, hopelessness, and cognitive avoidance. That item therefore sits awkwardly with both the node structure and the absence of any corresponding threat-related content elsewhere in the profile.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Constant Vigilance: I have to be especially careful because you never know what can happen next
issues.explanation: The Negative Appraisals node mixes three quite different themes—ongoing current danger/hypervigilance, severe depressive hopelessness, and moral/injustice-focused appraisal. These can coexist, but with only three appraisal items and no corresponding Threat or Trigger content, the node lacks a clear coherent theme tied to the formulation.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Life Not Worth Living: I am not sure my life is worth living anymore
issues.explanation: A prominent appraisal of current danger ('Constant Vigilance') would usually connect clinically with Threat and/or Trigger content, but both nodes are absent here and all edges involving Threat/Triggers are inactive. This makes that item poorly aligned with the stated formulation structure.

For a military trauma profile, loud noises are coherent, but alcohol smell and burnt smell together are hard to reconcile clinically without any corresponding memory, threat, or appraisal content indicating fire, explosions, intoxication, barracks/social-drinking contexts, or another olfactory-linked trauma scene. The trigger set implies a specific sensory trauma context that is not represented elsewhere in the profile.

The trigger profile is mostly coherent with military trauma (loud noises, burnt smell), but 'Babies' is hard to reconcile with the rest of the profile and trauma type because no memory, threat, appraisal, or strategy item suggests infant-related content or a civilian/family trauma context. This makes that trigger clinically hard to explain within the same trauma narrative.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: No Accountability: The people responsible have faced no consequences
issues.explanation: 'No Accountability' can occur after military trauma, but here the rest of the profile is dominated by sensory-perceptual trauma memory, generalized danger beliefs, and avoidance/distraction, with no other items indicating moral injury, betrayal, or injustice themes. Given the formulation strongly links Negative Appraisals to Memory and Maladaptive Strategies, this appraisal is insufficiently supported by the accompanying memory and strategy items and sits apart from the otherwise fear-based profile.

The trigger items are strongly combat-specific and plausibly fit military trauma, but the formulation marks all Triggers pathways as inactive, including Triggers → Threat, Triggers → Memory, and Triggers → Negative Appraisals. With three intense sensory trauma reminders selected, one would expect at least some linked threat or memory activation. As written, the trigger node is too active and trauma-specific to sit coherently as an isolated component in this formulation.

issues.item: Triggers: Olfactory Danger Cue: Burnt smell
issues.explanation: The appraisal items 'World is Dangerous' and 'I have to be on guard all the time' imply a persistent sense of current threat, yet Threat is entirely disconnected in the formulation and no Threat items are present. These appraisals can occur in PTSD, but together they function as threat-laden beliefs that sit awkwardly with a model where Negative Appraisals link mainly to Memory and Maladaptive Strategies rather than to current threat processing.

vignette:
Lukas had been 21 when he finally asked for help, a single man living back in his hometown after leaving the military and taking work as a bus driver. What brought him to treatment had roots in a combat incident he still struggled to speak about in any coherent way. He could say, in the barest terms, that there had been an explosion and that people had been hurt, but when he tried to tell it, the account broke apart. He remembered it in disconnected pieces that did not seem to join: the sudden sharpness of a burnt smell in the air; the jolt of sound when the blast went off; the whine of helicopters overhead afterward; flashes of dust, noise, movement, and other men shouting. When he tried to put those fragments into order, the scene would not settle into a full story. He would stop, stare ahead, and say he knew what had happened but could not find the words to describe it. At times it felt to him less like a memory than a film that had been left running somewhere in the background, playing over and over without his consent.

In the months after returning home, Lukas began to notice that certain moments could pull him straight back toward that scene. A burnt smell in particular made his body tense before he had even worked out where it was coming from. The first time it happened at work was on an ordinary route when the bus passed a street where someone had been burning rubbish in a metal barrel. The smell drifted in through the open door at a stop, and he gripped the wheel harder, suddenly certain that something was wrong. He found himself scanning the road and the mirrors, checking the sky whenever an aircraft passed overhead, and he would still go rigid at the sudden bang of a backfiring car or a slammed metal shutter. Helicopter sounds were especially hard to tolerate; even a distant aircraft could make him feel as though he had to get ready for something immediate and terrible. He came to believe that the world was a dangerous place and that he had to be on guard all the time, because the one time he had not been able to control what was happening had been enough to convince him that danger could arrive without warning.

That sense of threat altered the way he moved through daily life. Lukas began avoiding crowded places such as shopping centres and public events, not because he wanted to be alone exactly, but because crowds felt unmanageably exposed. Too many people, too much noise, too many ways for something to go wrong; he would scan exits before entering and leave early if the place started to fill up. He also stopped going to religious spaces and gatherings, even when family or acquaintances suggested he come along. The quiet expectation of standing among others in a church or hall made him uneasy, and he preferred not to put himself in a place where he could not easily watch what everyone else was doing. Over time, he spent long hours on his phone, games, or the internet, especially at night after work, not wanting the stillness that came when he was left with his own thoughts. The screen gave him something to focus on until he was tired enough to sleep, and it kept him from drifting into the same image-laden replay that could start without warning.

His work as a bus driver brought him into repeated contact with exactly the kinds of cues he tried to avoid. He still showed up and did his shifts, but there were days when a siren, an aircraft overhead, or the smell of something burnt on a route would make the cab feel suddenly too small. He would keep driving, jaw tight, attention split between the road and whatever he feared might be coming next. Outside of work, he found himself withdrawing from places where he might have to face those same sensations in public. Friends drifted because he declined invitations to busy venues or religious events, and he became more isolated, which only left him more time alone with the film-like loop in his mind. By the time he came for assessment, his score on the PTSD measure reflected how pervasive this had become.

Lukas did not present as someone looking for reassurance so much as someone worn down by constant alertness and by the growing conviction that his future had narrowed. He said he was not sure his life was worth living anymore, and although he did not speak in dramatic terms, there was a flatness in the way he said it that made it clear he had been sitting with that thought for some time. What finally brought him in was the sense that he could no longer keep doing the day-to-day work of holding himself together by distraction and vigilance. He was most afraid that he would always be waiting for the next bang, the next smell, the next sound overhead, and never feel safe again. At the same time, he was hoping that if he talked carefully enough, someone might help him make sense of what remained so fractured in his mind and give him a way to move through ordinary life without feeling as though he had to stand guard every minute of it.
